title: AI-Native Software Development
subtitle: Two skills in one roadmap: working with coding agents without losing your judgement, and building LLM-powered features that survive contact with production.

topics.label: How LLMs actually work (enough to not be fooled)
topics.desc: You do not need to train a model. You do need a working mental model of tokens, context windows, sampling and why the thing is confidently wrong sometimes. Skip this and every later decision is guesswork.

links.label: Karpathy: Intro to Large Language Models (1h video)

children.label: Tokens, context windows, cost
children.desc:
Everything is billed and limited in tokens (roughly 3/4 of a word in English, far worse for code and non-Latin scripts). The context window is the model's entire working memory for a request; nothing persists between calls unless you send it again.

Practical consequence: **context is a budget**. Learn to count it.

children.label: Sampling, temperature, determinism
children.desc: Outputs are sampled, not computed. Temperature 0 is *more* deterministic, not deterministic. Any test that asserts exact output strings will flake. Design for that from day one.

children.label: Hallucination and calibration
children.desc: Models produce plausible text, and plausibility is not truth. The fix is never "a better prompt" alone; it is grounding (give it the facts), tooling (let it look things up) and verification (check the output). Treat every claim from a model like a claim from a confident intern.

children.label: Build a tiny GPT yourself
children.desc: Karpathy's *Zero to Hero* series ends with you writing a small transformer from scratch. Around 10 hours. Not required, but nothing else demystifies the technology as thoroughly.

topics.label: Working with coding agents
topics.desc: Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and friends. The skill is not prompting; it is **delegation with verification**: giving the agent enough context to do the job and enough constraints that you can check the result.

children.label: Context files: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions
children.desc: A short file in the repo that tells the agent how this codebase works: build commands, test commands, conventions, what not to touch. This is the single highest-leverage thing you can do. Keep it under a page; agents read it every session.

faq.q: What goes in a good context file?
faq.a:
The things a new senior hire would ask in their first hour:

```
# Build & test
make test          # unit tests, must pass before any PR
make lint

# Conventions
- Errors are wrapped with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)
- No new dependencies without a note in the PR
- Migrations live in db/migrations, never edit an applied one
```

Not: your whole architecture doc. Link to it instead.

children.label: Plan, then execute
children.desc: For anything beyond a one-liner, ask for a plan first and read it. Most bad agent outcomes trace back to a wrong assumption that was visible in the plan. Approve, correct, then let it run.

children.label: Verification loops
children.desc: Give the agent a way to check its own work: a test command, a type checker, a linter, a screenshot. Agents with a feedback loop produce dramatically better code than agents writing blind. If your repo has no fast test command, fix that before adopting agents.

children.label: Test-first with an agent
children.desc: Write (or have it write) the failing test, confirm it fails, then ask for the implementation. Prevents the agent from "fixing" the test.

children.label: Review the diff like a stranger wrote it
children.desc: Because one did. Agent code has a particular failure shape: locally plausible, globally unaware. Look for duplicated helpers, ignored existing abstractions, and swallowed errors.

children.label: MCP: giving agents tools
children.desc: The Model Context Protocol is the standard way to expose your systems (issue tracker, database, internal APIs, docs) to any agent. Write one small MCP server for something your team uses daily; it will change how you think about agent workflows.

children.label: Security of agent workflows
children.desc: An agent that can read the web and run commands can be turned against you by content it reads (**prompt injection**). Rules: least-privilege tokens, sandboxed execution, no secrets in context, human approval for destructive actions, and never let an agent both read untrusted input and act with credentials in the same session without a boundary.

children.label: Skills and custom agents
children.desc: Reusable instruction bundles (Copilot agent files, Claude skills, Cursor rules) for recurring tasks: release notes, migration scaffolds, code review checklists. Worth it once you find yourself pasting the same prompt a third time.

links.label: VS Code: custom agents and prompt files

topics.label: Building LLM features
topics.desc: The API call is the easy part. Everything around it (grounding, structure, tools, failure handling) is where the engineering lives.

children.label: Prompting as an engineering discipline
children.desc: Prompts are code: version them, test them, review them. Learn the handful of techniques that reliably work (clear role and task, examples, explicit output format, asking for reasoning before the answer) and stop reading prompt-hack listicles.

children.label: Structured output and tool calling
children.desc: Never parse free text when you can ask for JSON against a schema. Every major API supports schema-constrained output and function/tool calling. This is how you connect a model to real systems safely: the model picks the tool and arguments, *your code* runs it.

faq.q: The model returns valid JSON but wrong values. Now what?
faq.a:
Schema enforcement guarantees shape, not truth. Add:

- validation of business rules after parsing (dates in range, ids that exist)
- a `confidence` or `reason` field the model must fill, which you can log and threshold
- a retry with the validation error fed back, capped at 2 attempts

children.label: RAG: retrieval-augmented generation
children.desc: Give the model the relevant documents at request time instead of hoping it memorised them. The pipeline is: chunk, embed, store, retrieve, rerank, generate. Most RAG failures are retrieval failures; measure retrieval quality separately from answer quality.

children.label: Chunking and embeddings
children.desc: Chunk by structure (headings, functions), not fixed character counts. Try two embedding models; the difference is often larger than any prompt change.

children.label: Hybrid search and reranking
children.desc: Vector search alone misses exact terms (error codes, ids). Combine with BM25 and rerank the top 20. Postgres with pgvector is enough for most teams; you do not need a dedicated vector database to start.

children.label: When not to RAG
children.desc: Small, stable corpora fit in the context window. Long-context models with prompt caching are often cheaper and better than a retrieval pipeline for under a few hundred pages.

children.label: Agents and workflows
children.desc: Start with a *workflow* (fixed steps, model at each step) before an *agent* (model decides the steps). Workflows are debuggable and predictable; agents are for open-ended tasks and cost more to make reliable. Most production systems are workflows with one or two agentic steps.

children.label: Local and open-weight models
children.desc: For airgapped environments, data residency, or cost at scale: Llama, Qwen, Mistral and Gemma families run on your own hardware via vLLM or Ollama. Expect a capability gap against frontier APIs; measure it on *your* tasks rather than benchmarks.

topics.label: Evals, observability and cost
topics.desc: If you cannot measure it, every prompt change is a coin flip. Evals are to LLM features what tests are to code, and most teams skip them until the first regression in production.

links.label: Hamel Husain: your AI product needs evals

children.label: Build an eval set from real traffic
children.desc: 50 to 200 real inputs with expected outputs or grading rubrics beats any synthetic benchmark. Add every production failure to it. Run it on every prompt and model change, in CI.

faq.q: How do I grade outputs that have no single right answer?
faq.a:
Three options, in increasing cost:

- **assertions**: contains X, valid JSON, under N tokens
- **LLM-as-judge** with a rubric, calibrated against ~30 human-graded examples so you know its agreement rate
- **human review** of a sample, weekly

Use all three; judge-only evals drift.

children.label: Tracing and logging
children.desc: Log every prompt, response, tool call, latency and token count with a trace id. You will need it for debugging, cost attribution and building the eval set. OpenTelemetry has GenAI semantic conventions; Langfuse and Phoenix are open source UIs on top.

children.label: Cost and latency engineering
children.desc: Prompt caching, smaller models for routing and classification, batching for offline work, streaming for anything user-facing. A feature that costs more than it saves gets switched off; know the unit economics before launch.

children.label: Guardrails and content safety
children.desc: Input and output filters, PII redaction, topic restrictions. Cheap to add, but they are not a substitute for the design rules in the security node above.

topics.label: Ship something
topics.desc: One end-to-end project teaches more than the rest of this roadmap combined.

children.label: Project: a doc-answering bot for one repo
children.desc: RAG over your team's README, ADRs and runbooks, exposed as an MCP server so any agent can use it. Include: an eval set of 30 real questions, tracing, and a cost dashboard. Ship it to three colleagues and watch them use it.

children.label: Project: agentic PR triage
children.desc: A workflow that reads a new PR, runs the tests, summarises the risk, and posts a comment. Never merges. Learn where the model helps and where a regex would have done.

children.label: Write the postmortem
children.desc: After two weeks in use: what did it get wrong, what did people stop trusting, what did it cost? This is the document that earns you the next project.
